nodes.label: Goldhammer et al. (1990) described 14 Jewish patients from 10 families of Iraqi or Iranian origin who had congenital myasthenia with facial malformations: an elongated face, mandibular prognathism with class III malocclusion, and a high-arched palate. Muscle weakness was mostly limited to ptosis, weakness of the facial and masticatory muscles, and fatigable speech. The course was mild and nonprogressive, and patients responded to cholinesterase inhibitors.

In the patients described by Goldhammer et al. (1990), antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor were absent. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz produced a decremental response, but a single nerve stimulus did not produce a repetitive compound muscle action potential.
EMG: decremental response of compound muscle action potential to repetitive nerve stimulation

Goldhammer et al. (1990) concluded that this newly recognized form of congenital myasthenia, which clusters by ethnicity and occurs with facial malformations, is inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder.

Goldhammer et al. (1990) suggested that the facial abnormalities could either result from the neuromuscular defect or be primary and unrelated to it. They noted that the defect in neuromuscular transmission had yet to be identified.

Zlotogora (1995) reported that congenital myasthenia gravis was among the diseases frequent in both the Iranian and Iraqi Jewish communities. Iranian Jews are an ancient community with a very high degree of inbreeding and strong ties to Babylonian Jewry in Iraq.

Menold et al. (1998) studied 5 families of Iranian Jewish origin with 6 affected individuals who had been diagnosed with a phenotypically unique form of congenital myasthenic syndrome. Four of the families were consanguineous, and all came from the same geographic region, so the authors considered it highly likely that they carried the same ancestral CMS mutation.

In 5 Iranian Jewish families with CMS, Menold et al. (1998) excluded linkage to the regions on chromosomes 2 and 17 that contain the AChR subunit genes. They also excluded linkage to the chromosome 17p region to which familial infantile myasthenia had been mapped. The authors suggested that the clinical differences among patients with CMS correlate with locus heterogeneity, and that a defect in a different gene causes CMS in these patients.

Ohno et al. (2002) studied 4 patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate acetylcholine receptor (AChR) deficiency who had no mutations in AChR subunit genes. In each case, endplate studies showed decreased staining for rapsyn and AChR and impaired postsynaptic morphological development.
Abnormal synaptic transmission at the neuromuscular junction

nodes.label: impaired postsynaptic morphological development at the endplate

Ohno et al. (2002) identified 3 recessive RAPSN mutations in 4 patients with endplate AChR deficiency: 1 patient was compound heterozygous for L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; 2 patients were homozygous for N88K; and 1 patient was compound heterozygous for N88K and a 553ins5 frameshift in TPR5.

Ohno et al. (2002) found that the RAPSN N88K mutation, located in TPR3, was present in all 4 patients: homozygous in 2, and compound heterozygous with L14P in 1 and with 553ins5 in 1. In HEK cell expression studies, N88K did not hinder rapsyn self-association but diminished coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.

Ohno et al. (2002) identified a RAPSN L14P mutation in TPR1, compound heterozygous with N88K, in 1 patient with endplate AChR deficiency. In HEK cell expression studies, the mutation did not hinder rapsyn self-association but diminished coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.

Ohno et al. (2002) identified a 5-bp insertion in RAPSN (553ins5), which causes a frameshift in TPR5, compound heterozygous with N88K, in 1 patient with endplate AChR deficiency. In HEK cell expression studies, the mutation did not hinder rapsyn self-association but diminished coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.

Ohno et al. (2002) noted that rapsyn is essential for clustering AChR at the endplate. Its 7 TPRs mediate self-association, a coiled-coil domain binds AChR, and a RING-H2 domain binds beta-dystroglycan. Expression studies showed that the patient mutations did not hinder rapsyn self-association but did diminish coclustering of AChR with rapsyn. This indicated that the endplate AChR deficiency results from impaired rapsyn-mediated AChR clustering.

Ohno et al. (2002) noted that many CMSs with endplate AChR deficiency had been traced to mutations in AChR subunit genes, but in a subset of patients the genetic defect had remained unknown. They found that rapsyn mutations cause some of these cases.

In a patient (patient 1) with congenital myasthenic syndrome, Ohno et al. (2003) identified a -27C-G mutation in the RAPSN promoter region that changes an E-box at -27 to -22 from CAGCTG to GAGCTG. The allele harboring the mutation was not transcribed in the patient's muscle. Electrophoretic mobility shift assays showed that -27C-G lost binding affinity for components of C2C12 myotube nuclear extracts, and luciferase reporter assays showed attenuated reporter expression in C2C12 myotubes and in MyoD- or myogenin-transfected HEK cells; the mutation also markedly attenuated the enhancer activity of an E-box on an SV40 promoter.

Ohno et al. (2003) identified a -38A-G mutation in the RAPSN promoter in patients 2 through 8 with congenital myasthenic syndrome, all of Oriental Jewish stock of Iraqi or Iranian origin. The mutation changes an E-box at -40 to -35 from CAACTG to CAGCTG without affecting the CANNTG consensus. Electrophoretic mobility shift assays showed that -38A-G gained binding affinity for components of C2C12 myotube nuclear extracts, and luciferase reporter assays showed attenuated reporter expression in C2C12 myotubes. The authors predicted that impaired RAPSN promoter transcriptional activity would reduce rapsyn expression and cause endplate acetylcholine receptor deficiency.
Ohno et al. (2003) reported that the 7 congenital myasthenic syndrome patients carrying the RAPSN -38A-G promoter mutation, all Oriental Jews of Iraqi or Iranian origin, had facial malformations.
Haplotype analysis by Ohno et al. (2003) showed that the RAPSN -38A-G promoter mutation in Oriental Jewish patients of Iraqi or Iranian origin arose from a common founder.
Ohno et al. (2003) determined that the major transcriptional start site of RAPSN lies 172 nucleotides upstream of the translational start site.
Burke et al. (2003) identified rapsyn mutations in 16 unrelated patients with congenital/hereditary myasthenic syndrome. All of them carried the N88K mutation.

Burke et al. (2003) described two distinct phenotypes in 16 unrelated patients with rapsyn-related congenital myasthenic syndrome: early onset and late onset. The early-onset form was often associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and life-threatening crises. The late-onset form began in adolescence or adulthood and was at first mistaken for seronegative myasthenia gravis.
Burke et al. (2003) noted that recognizing the late-onset rapsyn phenotype, which can be mistaken for seronegative myasthenia gravis, should prevent inappropriate immunotherapy.

Dunne and Maselli (2004) used 7 intragenic SNPs spanning 8 kb of the rapsyn (RAPSN) gene to characterize the haplotype associated with the N88K mutation. They found a common haplotype in 3 affected N88K homozygotes that was present in all heterozygous carriers of N88K, and concluded that this supported a founder effect.

Dunne and Maselli (2004) found 2 asymptomatic individuals homozygous for the rapsyn N88K mutation who carried a second haplotype that differed at 3 SNP sites downstream of the mutation. The authors suggested that recombination events may have occurred within the rapsyn gene and that this may have implications for the phenotypic expression of the disease.
Müller et al. (2004) concluded that the congenital myasthenic syndrome mutation RAPSN N88K derives from an ancient Indo-European founder.

Gaudon et al. (2010) described 3 patients who had a typical recessive congenital myasthenic syndrome phenotype and mutations in the RAPSN gene. Family analysis showed that direct sequencing had missed one mutant allele in each patient. Allelic quantification of the patients' DNA found 3 novel multiexon deletions in RAPSN.

Gaudon et al. (2010) found that the 3 genomic rearrangements accounted for 15% of their CMS patients with RAPSN mutations. They emphasized that SNP markers and a gene dosage method should be used alongside direct DNA sequencing, particularly when genetic counseling is at issue.

Das et al. (2014) reported a 20-month-old boy with rapsyn deficiency who presented at birth with weak cry, hypotonia, joint contractures, and facial deformity. Because of respiratory difficulty associated with muscle fatigue, he spent 71 days in the neonatal intensive care unit and 47 days in the pediatric intensive care unit. Imaging, metabolic tests, and electrodiagnostic studies were normal, and muscle biopsy showed myofiber atrophy in a pattern consistent with early denervation.

In a boy with congenital myasthenic syndrome in whom extensive testing, including microarray, was nondiagnostic, Das et al. (2014) identified 2 pathogenic mutations in the RAPSN gene by whole-exome sequencing.

Das et al. (2014) treated their patient with RAPSN-related congenital myasthenic syndrome with pyridostigmine at 16 months of age, resulting in dramatic improvement in muscle tone and strength and steady resolution of joint contractures; 4 months later he was beginning to bear weight, could sit unsupported, and vocalized full words.

In their review, Engel et al. (2015) stated that most patients with CMS due to rapsyn deficiency present in the first year of life and a few present later. Nearly one-third have arthrogryposis at birth and other congenital malformations. Intercurrent infections or fever can trigger respiratory crises leading to anoxic encephalopathy. The clinical features can suggest autoimmune myasthenia gravis, but the ocular ductions are intact in most patients.

Engel et al. (2015) reported that in rapsyn deficiency, multiple synaptic contacts appear on single muscle fibers. The endplate AChR deficiency is milder than in primary AChR deficiency, and the junctional folds are poorly differentiated. Different RAPSN mutations hinder rapsyn self-association or binding to AChR, impede agrin-MuSK-LRP4-mediated clustering of AChR, or decrease rapsyn expression.

Engel et al. (2015) summarized that rapsyn concentrates and anchors AChR in the postsynaptic membrane and is required for development of the junctional folds. They described its domains: a myristoylated N-terminal region that links it to the membrane; 7 tetratricopeptide repeats needed for self-aggregation and MuSK binding; a coiled-coil domain that interacts with AChR subunits; and a C-terminal domain that binds beta-dystroglycan.
Engel et al. (2015) noted that Indo-Europeans carry a common N88K mutation in RAPSN. Other mutations occur in the promoter region and throughout the RAPSN open reading frame.

Engel et al. (2015) stated that rapsyn deficiency shows no genotype-phenotype correlations, with one exception. Near-Eastern Jewish patients homozygous for the E-box mutation c.-38A>G have a mild phenotype with ptosis, prognathism, severe masticatory and facial muscle weakness, and hypernasal speech.

Engel et al. (2015) reported that most patients with rapsyn deficiency respond well to AChE inhibitors. Some get additional benefit from 3,4-diaminopyridine, and some from adding ephedrine or albuterol.
Engel et al. (2015) classified 356 index patients with CMS investigated at the Mayo Clinic between 1988 and 2014. Rapsyn deficiency accounted for 51 index cases (14.3%).

Engel et al. (2015) listed phenotypic clues pointing to rapsyn deficiency: congenital contractures, and sudden apneic episodes provoked by fever or stress. They added that apneic episodes also occur with ChAT mutations and Na-channel myasthenia, and that limb-girdle and axial weakness is occasionally seen with rapsyn mutations.
Apneic episodes precipitated by illness, fatigue, stress
